clue.text: Bully’s given a toss, a great

definitions.note: an exclamation of delight, read as the cry 'great!'

blocks.note: to cow someone is to bully or intimidate them
A plus BUNG, informal British for a throw or toss
taken as written

explanation.surface: A bully is getting a good shaking, and someone thinks that is great.
explanation.walkthrough: Bung is a British colloquialism for throw; the second article stands alone just before the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Cowabunga is a surfer's whoop of exhilaration, used as a cry meaning roughly 'brilliant!'

clue.text: Go over to the audience for some language

indicators.note: what is delivered to an audience is heard rather than read, so the sound counts

blocks.note: to go over something is to check it

explanation.surface: A speaker reviewing a text with listeners in order to teach them a foreign tongue.
explanation.walkthrough: The spelling with Z sounds exactly like the verb meaning to examine.
explanation.definitionFit: Czech is the Slavic tongue spoken in the Czech Republic, one example among many.

indicators.note: one thing in another sits inside it, so the second piece wraps the first

blocks.note: a hoop is a circular band, as on a barrel
wee is Scottish for small or short

explanation.surface: Praise for a music group, summed up briefly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Band' tempts the solver toward a pop group such as The Who, but here it is a ring of metal; 'in short' is container plus a word for small.
explanation.definitionFit: Whoopee is an exclamation of joy, the kind of cry that means 'great!'

blocks.note: first meaning: British slang short for brilliant
second meaning: a European flatfish related to the turbot

explanation.walkthrough: 'Swimmer' is a common crossword way of pointing to a fish.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is clipped British slang for excellent and also the name of an edible flatfish.

clue.text: Undoing last of knots I identified from below, male cuts through it

indicators.note: the last of anything is its final element, so only the end letter is kept
in a down entry, reading from the bottom upward runs the letters backwards
something that cuts through another ends up lodged in its middle

blocks.note: final letter of the word
taken as written
something identified has been seen or spotted
M is the standard abbreviation for male

explanation.surface: Someone untying knots, working from the bottom, while a man slices through them.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Undoing' looks like part of the knot picture but is the definition, in the sense of a person's ruin.
explanation.definitionFit: A nemesis is the agent of someone's downfall, so it is their ruin or undoing.

clue.text: Same absurd ideas crushed by a pro

indicators.note: something absurd makes no sense, so these letters need setting into a sensible order
in a down entry, what is crushed by something sits underneath it

blocks.note: taken as written
pro means in favour of, that is, for
taken as written, then rearranged

explanation.surface: The same silly notions get flattened by an expert.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pro' suggests a professional, but it is the Latin preposition meaning in favour of.
explanation.definitionFit: Aforesaid means mentioned earlier, which in formal writing refers back to the same thing already named.

indicators.note: banks line a river on both sides, so one piece lines another

blocks.note: fab is slang short for fabulous
L is the standard abbreviation for left

explanation.surface: A business news headline: big banks have abandoned a corporation.
explanation.walkthrough: Banks and corporation set up a financial picture, but corporation is old British slang for a large belly.
explanation.definitionFit: A corporation, jokingly, is a pot belly, and excess body fat around the middle is flab.

clue.text: Discharge of gas leaving a system when running

indicators.note: whatever is leaving goes away, so that letter drops out

blocks.note: gas in the sense of wind from the gut
a leak is an escape or discharge, here losing its A

explanation.surface: An engineer's description of gas escaping from some kind of pipe network.
explanation.walkthrough: Read 'discharge of gas' as the gas's leak, so the gas word comes first; then the A goes, leaving a Swedish training term.
explanation.definitionFit: Fartlek is a Swedish method of training runners by mixing fast and slow running bursts.

clue.text: Literary similarity great, small issue with article penned

indicators.note: to be penned is to be shut inside an enclosure, so one piece is kept within another

blocks.note: ace is slang for excellent
S is the abbreviation for small
issue means offspring, such as a son
an is the indefinite article

explanation.surface: A critic notes a great likeness between texts, with a minor quibble about a published article.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Issue' sounds like a magazine edition alongside 'article', but it means offspring.
explanation.definitionFit: Assonance is the repetition of vowel sounds in nearby words, a resemblance of sound used in poetry.

clue.text: Skirt-wearing scholar lives for the pursuit of titillation

indicators.note: a garment that is being worn wraps around its wearer

blocks.note: a hem is the edge or skirt of a cloth
a don is a university teacher at Oxford or Cambridge
is means exists or lives

explanation.surface: A cross-dressing academic who lives for cheap thrills.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Skirt-wearing' reads as one adjective, but it splits into a word for an edge plus the container signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Hedonism is the devotion to pleasure, so it is a life spent chasing thrills and excitement.

blocks.note: a machine that is running is on
a rush is a marsh plant

explanation.surface: A gardener's note on the progress of a creeping plant.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Running plant' looks like one botanical phrase, as for a climber or runner bean, but splits into two pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: An onrush is a surging forward movement, a headlong advance by a crowd or force.

clue.text: Place of worship, holy building last of all visited by primate

indicators.note: the last of anything is its end, so only the final letter is kept
a place visited by someone has that guest inside it

blocks.note: CH is the abbreviation for church
final letter of the word
an ape is a primate

explanation.surface: A church receives a visit from an archbishop, the primate of the land.
explanation.walkthrough: A primate is also a senior archbishop, which suits the church picture; here it is the animal.
explanation.definitionFit: A chapel is a small church or a room set aside for prayer and services.

blocks.note: first meaning: of excellent quality
second meaning: an example of the answer to 17 down, money

explanation.walkthrough: The cross-reference points to the entry at 17 down; British currency is one example of it.
explanation.definitionFit: Sterling describes first-rate work, and is also British money, a form of capital.

indicators.note: to review is to look back over, so the letters run backwards

blocks.note: vol is the abbreviation for volume
a see is a bishop's diocese, and Ely in Cambridgeshire is one

explanation.surface: A critic's verdict: a great book, reviewed; go and look.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Reviewed' fits the book-critic picture but signals a reversal; 'see' is not the verb but a bishop's seat, here the cathedral city of Ely.
explanation.definitionFit: Lovely is an everyday British expression of approval meaning wonderful or excellent.

indicators.note: letters that are moving shift out of their places into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A schemer is relocating to a café.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Manipulator' suggests a schemer, but it is meant literally: someone who manipulates bones and joints.
explanation.definitionFit: An osteopath treats patients by physically manipulating the spine, muscles and joints with the hands.

clue.text: Call love and desire quite fair?

blocks.note: to yell is to call out
love is zero in tennis, shaped like O
a wish is a desire

explanation.surface: Is it fair to label love and desire the same thing?
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fair' seems to mean just, but it refers to light colouring, as in fair hair.
explanation.definitionFit: Fair hair or skin is pale, somewhat blond, so a fairish tint is tending to yellow.

blocks.note: first meaning: very fine or impressive
second meaning: a smacking on the bottom

explanation.walkthrough: The adjective sense, as in 'spanking new', is informal British.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means excellent or brisk as an adjective, and as a noun a physical chastisement of a child.

clue.text: Second feather, say, one splitting hairs?

blocks.note: S is the abbreviation for second
a feather is an example of something used to tickle

explanation.surface: A feather used to split a hair, as if for a fussy experiment.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Say' marks the feather as just one example of the thing.
explanation.definitionFit: A stickler insists on exactness about trivial details, which is what pedantic hair-splitting means.

blocks.note: first meaning: an old-fashioned British exclamation of approval
second meaning: wealth or assets available for use

explanation.walkthrough: 'Capital!' is a dated British way of saying excellent.
explanation.definitionFit: Capital is the money and assets a business or person has available, and also means first-rate.

blocks.note: first meaning: old British schoolboy slang for splendid
second meaning: the act of tearing apart

explanation.surface: Something great has been wrecked.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ripping' as praise is dated British slang, as in a ripping yarn.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is old slang for splendid, and as a noun it is the tearing of something to pieces.

indicators.note: what is reported is passed on by word of mouth, so the sound counts

blocks.note: a duct is a pipe or channel

explanation.surface: News reports say a pipe gave way abruptly.
explanation.walkthrough: The past tense of the verb sounds the same as the word for a tube carrying air or fluid.
explanation.definitionFit: To duck is to drop or lower the head quickly, so someone who did so dropped low abruptly.

blocks.note: cor is a British exclamation of surprise, like gee
a king is a man on a chessboard

explanation.surface: An excited cry of approval: great, wow, man!
explanation.walkthrough: 'Gee man!' reads as one American exclamation, but each word gives a piece; a chess piece is often called a man.
explanation.definitionFit: Corking is dated British slang for excellent, a cheerful word of approval.

clue.text: Great romance with piano in a duet?

blocks.note: to romance someone is to woo them
p is the musical abbreviation for piano, softly
a duet has two performers, so the same pair of pieces comes twice

explanation.surface: A love song performed with piano as a duet sounds great.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Piano' and 'duet' set a musical scene; the piano gives one letter and the duet doubles everything.
explanation.definitionFit: Woop woop is an informal cry of excitement or celebration, much like shouting 'brilliant!'

blocks.note: first meaning: hippie-era slang for excellent
second meaning, taken literally: a long way from the centre

explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags the literal reading of a slang phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: Remote country districts lie a long distance away from town, and the same phrase is also slang for wonderful.

indicators.note: about means around, so one piece is placed round the other

blocks.note: to stuff is to fill
R is the abbreviation for right

explanation.surface: Fussy detailing on something that is more or less correct.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Detail' is a noun meaning a decorative extra, not the verb.
explanation.definitionFit: A frill is an unnecessary decorative extra, a small ornamental touch added for show.

clue.text: Dark, one allowing in minimum of luminescence

indicators.note: the minimum of a word is its smallest part, a single opening letter
allowing something in admits it inside, so one piece holds another

blocks.note: a unit is one
first letter of the word

explanation.surface: A dark room that lets in just the faintest glow.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface invites a light-related answer from 'luminescence', but only its opening letter is used.
explanation.definitionFit: Something unlit has no lamp or light switched on, so it is in darkness.

clue.text: Cocktail, one ruined by gin, vermouth perfect

blocks.note: gin is nicknamed mother's ruin, so the one it ruins is mother, MA
IT is short for Italian vermouth, as in gin and it
A1 means first-rate, with the 1 standing as I

explanation.surface: A cocktail recipe: one drink spoiled by gin, but the vermouth is just right.
explanation.walkthrough: Gin has the British nickname mother's ruin; 'gin and it' is a classic British drink of gin with Italian sweet vermouth.
explanation.definitionFit: A mai tai is a rum-based mixed drink with lime and orange liqueur, from tiki bars.

indicators.note: a scribble is messy writing, so the letters come out jumbled

blocks.note: II is two in Roman numerals
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone has scrawled the dictator's name twice and asks if that makes his monogram.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition gains a twist from the surface: Joseph Stalin's own monogram letters would be J and S.
explanation.definitionFit: J and S are the first letters of a name such as Joseph Stalin, an example of a monogram.

indicators.note: food that is fed to someone goes inside them

blocks.note: amigo is Spanish for friend, a pal
H is the abbreviation for hot, as on taps

explanation.surface: A friend is served a fiery curry.
explanation.walkthrough: The first 'hot' is the letter inserted; the second belongs to the definition. Phal is a British curry-house dish.
explanation.definitionFit: Phal is reputedly the fiercest dish on British Indian restaurant menus, hotter than vindaloo.

blocks.note: something raised is high
white is an example of a light colour

explanation.surface: A white flag goes up, perhaps signalling surrender.
explanation.walkthrough: The white flag of surrender is the picture, but 'flag' is a verb meaning to mark for attention.
explanation.definitionFit: To flag a passage is to mark it out for attention, as one does with a marker pen.
